content: Depth of field (DOF) in optics, particularly in photography and cinematography, refers to the range of distance in a scene where objects appear acceptably sharp in an image. A lens can only focus precisely at one specific distance, but the transition from sharp to unsharp is gradual. This means that within the DOF, the lack of sharpness is not noticeable under normal viewing conditions. For certain types of photography, such as landscapes, a large DOF is often desirable to keep most of the scene in focus. Conversely, for portraits or close-ups, a shallow DOF is preferred to isolate the subject from the background. The DOF is influenced by three main factors: the distance to the subject, the focal length of the lens, and the lens aperture (f-number). At close distances, the subject magnification and f-number primarily determine the DOF. Increasing the magnification, either by moving closer to the subject or using a lens with a longer focal length, reduces the DOF. Conversely, decreasing the magnification increases the DOF. For a given subject magnification, increasing the f-number (reducing the aperture size) increases the DOF, while decreasing the f-number reduces it. When the lens is focused at the hyperfocal distance, the DOF extends from half the hyperfocal distance to infinity, providing the maximum possible DOF for a given f-number. Digital photography has introduced new methods to control DOF, including techniques that allow adjustments after the image is captured or achieve DOF effects that are impossible with traditional methods. Precise focus is achieved at only one distance, where a point object produces a point image. At other distances, the object is defocused, creating a blur spot shaped like the lens aperture, typically assumed to be circular. If this blur spot is small enough, it is indistinguishable from a point and appears sharp, referred to as acceptably sharp. The largest blur spot that still appears sharp is called the circle of confusion. The size of this circle depends on factors such as visual acuity, viewing conditions, and the degree of image enlargement. The transition from sharp to unsharp is gradual, so the boundaries of the DOF are not rigid. Factors like subject movement, the nature of the subject, and the distance from the camera also influence when defocus becomes noticeable. The acceptable circle of confusion varies with image format size, as larger formats require less magnification for projection, affecting the perceived sharpness. In motion pictures, larger film formats require longer focal lengths to achieve the same framing as smaller formats, resulting in a smaller DOF. For example, a 50mm lens on 16mm film, a 100mm lens on 35mm film, and a 250mm lens on 65mm film provide similar framing but different DOF characteristics. Larger formats inherently have a shallower DOF, necessitating adjustments in exposure, framing, or subject distance to match the appearance of smaller formats. The f-number of a lens controls the DOF for a given subject framing. Increasing the f-number (reducing the aperture size) increases the DOF but reduces the amount of light entering the lens and increases diffraction, which limits how much the aperture can be reduced. In cinematography, consistent image quality often requires fixed aperture settings, with exposure adjusted using filters or lighting. In still photography, aperture settings are more frequently adjusted to achieve creative effects with DOF. Camera movements, such as tilt and swing, allow the plane of focus (POF) to be rotated, altering the shape and distribution of the DOF. When the POF is rotated, the near and far limits of the DOF are no longer parallel, creating a wedge-shaped DOF. This technique can be used to maximize or minimize the area of an image that is in focus. To achieve maximum DOF, many lenses include DOF scales that indicate the range of acceptable sharpness for a given focus distance and f-number. By aligning the infinity mark on the distance scale with the appropriate f-number mark, the lens can be set to the hyperfocal distance, maximizing the DOF. Selective focus, or differential focus, uses a limited DOF to emphasize a specific part of an image while de-emphasizing the background. This technique is common in portrait photography and artistic compositions. The degree of background blur depends on the distance from the plane of focus, the lens focal length, and the f-number. Adjusting these parameters can help achieve the desired balance between subject sharpness and background blur. The distribution of DOF is not symmetrical; the DOF beyond the subject is always greater than the DOF in front of it. At the hyperfocal distance, the far DOF extends to infinity. As the subject distance decreases, the near-to-far DOF ratio approaches unity at high magnifications. DOF formulas are based on several assumptions, including paraxial optics and negligible lens aberrations. While these simplifications are generally adequate for most applications, they may introduce errors in specific scenarios, such as close-up or macro photography. Additionally, diffraction limits the extent to which the aperture can be reduced to increase DOF, requiring a trade-off between center and edge sharpness. In practical terms, achieving the desired DOF often involves balancing various factors, including subject distance, lens focal length, and aperture size. Understanding these principles allows photographers to make informed decisions to achieve their creative and technical goals.
